at a glance - the philippines improved its reading mathematics and science rankings in the programme for international student assessment - education officials emphasize the need to sustain this momentum and continue reforms manila philippines the philippines performance in the programme for international student assessment pisa improved in with the country climbing out of the bottom in the subjects covered the philippines ranked 72nd out of countries in reading 74th out of countries in mathematics and 77th out of countries in science according to the pisa results released on tuesday september the organisation for economic co-operation and development oecd which conducts the test found that filipino students had average scores of in science up by points from the previous pisa edition in mathematics up by points and in reading up by points the oecd described the philippines as the fastest improving country in terms of reading performance the department of education deped noted that this is the philippines strongest pisa performance to date since the country first joined the global assessment in and again in where it saw dismal results both times although an improvement it should be seen as a starting point and highlights the work that remains added the deped this is a significant achievement for our learners and for the entire philippine education system but more than the numbers we are seeing evidence that our learners are capable of making real and meaningful progress education secretary sonny angara said in a press release we should be proud of how far our learners and teachers have come but we should be even more determined about how much farther we can go in the philippines was ranked lowest in reading and second to the last in science and mathematics four years after that the philippines was still among the bottom the second congressional commission on education said the task now is to sustain the momentum stressing that education reforms require consistency of purpose continuity in implementation and the commitment of the entire country according to the oecd or around two in three filipino students were low performers in science mathematics and reading in in the edition the oecd also assessed students on computational problem solving or the ability of students to solve problems using modeling or programming tools and practices such as conducting experiments analyzing data and building and debugging computational artifacts the philippines scored below the oecd average of learning recovery in a press conference after the announcement angara attributed the improved pisa performance to deped reforms such as reducing the administrative work of teachers improving curricula and emphasizing remediation angara replaced vice president sara duterte as education secretary in he inherited sectoral issues such as poor performance of filipino students in global assessments low literacy rates and calls to either review or scrap the k to program pisa was conducted in the early stages of the academic recovery and accessible learning aral program the country s national learning recovery initiative but by the end of school year - or after the first full-year implementation of the aral program around half of filipino students were still not proficient in reading according to the deped s own literacy assessment angara said the first year of aral which focused on reading was very encouraging the deped is also preparing to roll out sessions for mathematics soon it s only the second year so let s iterate change the approach if we see things that need to be improved he said in a mix of english and filipino however under the current budget proposal the aral program may have zero funding in asked whether the pisa results could make lawmakers rethink the deped budget angara replied sana i hope so extra preparations after the poor performance in and the deped took extra measures to prepare for pisa read why philippines pisa preparation is flawed according to the deped around -year-old students from schools in the philippines took part in pisa through a computer-based assessment most of the participating schools were regular public schools but there were also public science-oriented schools and private schools angara said the deped made sure that public schools would have at least one computer so as not to repeat the experience of participating students only encountering the technology for the first time during the test the private sector also helped in computerizing pisa-like tests to help students become familiar with the nature of the global assessment education undersecretary malcolm garma added that they made sure students would have good psychosocial well-being during the test with parents and local officials also engaged however the alliance of concerned teachers warned the public against an obsession with international rankings saying that pisa s framework reflects a westernized colonial perspective on education that fails to capture local realities global top performers the average scores among oecd countries for were in science in mathematics and in reading globally the chinese jurisdictions of beijing shanghai jiangsu and zhejiang along with singapore were the highest performers across science mathematics and reading in also among the top performing education systems in all three subjects were estonia japan korea macau china chinese taipei and the united kingdom but while the philippines had encouraging results pisa recorded the lowest oecd-average performance observed so far in science reading and mathematics pisa shows that reversing declines in student performance is urgent the most successful education systems focus on fewer areas in greater depth invest in teachers engage parents and provide targeted support for the students and schools that need it the most oecd secretary-general mathias cormann said in a press release catholic education authorities are calling for the immediate release of delayed government voucher funds saying many private schools are still awaiting subsidy disbursements even after the school year ended in early april the catholic educational association of the philippines ceap and the cbcp episcopal commission on catholic education ecce urged the department of education and the department of budget and management to expedite release of remaining subsidies in a joint appeal the groups said a considerable number of private schools especially small and financially vulnerable institutions have yet to receive educational service contracting esc subsidies and senior high school voucher program assistance for students they said the delays persist despite the end of school year leaving schools dependent on funds they described as essential for basic operations and financial stability catholic school officials warned that rising electricity costs and other operating expenses are further tightening already strained budgets in many private institutions the continued delay has placed serious strain on school finances at a time when institutions are already preparing for the next academic year the statement said the groups said unpaid subsidies are now affecting salaries benefits utilities and other obligations for both teaching and non-teaching personnel nationwide they added that government assistance remains a lifeline for many schools serving low-income communities and relying heavily on voucher programs to stay operational citing republic act no they stressed that the state recognizes private schools as partners in expanding access to education and easing congestion in public schools the spirit and intent of the law affirm the principle of public-private complementarity in education and underscore the state s commitment to sustaining the viability of private schools that help decongest the public education system the groups said ceap and ecce urged school operations and ensure teachers staff and learners are not further affected

read this in the manila times digital edition when geopolitics invades the classroom education stops being a bridge between peoples and risks becoming another battlefield of suspicion and bigotry when teachers scholars and students are viewed primarily through a national security lens rather than on the basis of evidence knowledge itself can become collateral damage confucius offered an enduring reminder to know what you know and to know what you do not know that is knowledge applied to the philippines today this confucian wisdom is especially relevant amid the marcos administration s hostile heightened scrutiny of chinese citizens institutions and china-related activities in the name of national security genuine security concerns deserve investigation but wisdom and responsible statecraft require distinguishing what is established from what is merely suspected institutional connections may warrant scrutiny they are not by themselves proof of espionage subversion or disloyalty when suspicion begins substituting for evidence the danger is that national security ceases to protect the classroom and instead allows geopolitics to colonize it the classroom new geopolitical frontline apparently the philippines has discovered a new frontline in the great geopolitical struggle of the 21st century not the south china sea not scarborough shoal not second thomas shoal but the classroom the strategic targets chinese schools in the philippines and the teaching of the mandarin language after months of increasingly securitized rhetoric about practically anything connected with china defense secretary gilberto gibo teodoro jr has now turned his attention to educational exchanges scholarships chinese-language programs and academic partnerships perhaps his next national security operation will be to inspect dictionaries especially chinese-english and filipino-chinese editions after all if mandarin itself is becoming suspicious who knows what dangerous geopolitical secrets might be hiding between a and z how profoundly pathetic the controversy started after sealight director ray powell a central intelligence agency cia operative in the philippines published an article alleging that chinese institutions connected with the so-called communist party s united front have developed extensive relationships with chinese-language schools and filipino-chinese organizations powell argues that teacher training educational cooperation and cultural programs can function as channels through which beijing promotes its narratives and political perspectives conveniently for powell his narrative soon found a government official megaphone a louder one at that full of suspicion no evidence or proof but offered by the philippine defense secretary himself gibo did not merely echo the bigot s alarmist anti-china rhetoric he amplified it warning that educational exchanges could supposedly provide china a foothold and opportunities to gather information and voilà academic exchanges between the philippines and china are suddenly recast as a national security suspect and vulnerability what a ridiculous geopolitical hysteria masquerading as analysis or intelligence at this rate one wonders whether the next great national security threat that gibo and powell will suspect will be a confucius or sun tzu quotation written on a classroom blackboard goodness gracious recalling chinese teachers but on a serious note mind you when insinuation travels from a cia operative in the philippines to the mouth of the defense secretary speculation acquires the costume of official intelligence except there is a rather obvious problem once gibo repeatedly places teachers scholars academic exchanges and cultural organizations inside a national security frame there may be consequences on oct the immaculate conception academy informed parents that the ffcccii federation of filipino chinese chambers of commerce and industry inc had advised it that its chinese teachers needed to return to china immediately jubilee christian academy separately announced that its chinese volunteer teachers had been unexpectedly recalled by their sending organization both schools began scrambling for substitute teachers online instruction and other arrangements on oct it was reported that something potentially much larger had happened ffcccii and other relevant philippines-chinese educational institutions in consultation and coordination with the chinese embassy in manila had decided to withdraw chinese volunteers and dispatched teachers from chinese schools nationwide reports indicate roughly teachers were leaving and the decision was attributed to safety concerns raised by teachers families following the attacks and allegations surrounding chinese-language education citing articles by powell in sealight about chinese-language schools and recent statements by gibo it was further reported that the decision came from the inviting organizations not an expulsion by manila or an order from beijing just as a caveat these reports still require independent confirmation from the organizations concerned collateral damage seriously speaking this turn of events is deeply counterproductive the collateral damage from indiscriminate suspicion and insinuation coming from the defense secretary himself could be considerable fewer scholarships visiting professors language teachers academic conferences research collaborations scientific partnerships and professional exchanges between the philippines and china worse it creates a chilling effect where filipino academics begin wondering whether studying china speaking mandarin collaborating with chinese universities or attending conferences there will make their patriotism and nationalism suspect there is nothing objectionable about examining foreign-funded programs but there is an important line between investigating specific evidence and treating association with china or anything chinese as suspicion or evidence of wrongdoing influence operations or espionage a mandarin teacher is not automatically an influence operative a filipino scholar attending a chinese university or attending conferences held in china is not therefore an agent of beijing a philippine university or school partnership with china does not by itself constitute espionage national security deserves vigilance but accusations require evidence proof there is an enormous logical distance between foreign influence exists and educational engagement with china is presumptively suspicious that distinction seems increasingly blurred by people like powell and gibo and this is where national security discourse becomes intellectually lazy and dishonest connections are not crimes associations are not evidence of espionage and studying another civilization is not disloyalty to one s country national security requires evidence not suspicion vigilance not paranoia and sinophobia and sound intelligence not guilt by association take note department of education-national capital region deped-ncr records show that chinese-language instruction is not some mysterious underground operation discovered yesterday by counterintelligence sleuths the government itself has maintained a special program in foreign language-chinese including teacher training and mentoring deped documentation explains that chinese volunteer teachers have served as trainers for prospective filipino mandarin teachers and that the training structure included philippine instruction and immersion programs in china conclusion the philippines absolutely should protect itself against espionage covert foreign interference or influence and disinformation from any country but national security cannot become a magic phrase that transforms speculation into evidence and classrooms into counterintelligence theaters the philippines should stop allowing an entire universe of legitimate educational exchanges with china to exist beneath a cloud of insinuation and suspicion because when geopolitical suspicion reaches the classroom everyone eventually loses the philippines loses language expertise scholarships research partnerships and access to one of the world s largest academic systems china countries may disagree over geopolitics but education should remain a bridge not become another casualty of it perhaps confucius offers the lesson our defense establishment most needs wisdom begins by knowing the difference between what you know and what you merely suspect in national security confusing the two does not make a country safer it can simply make ignorance an official government policy

at a glance - the author enrolled in certificate courses at the development academy of the philippines to gain knowledge in geopolitics international relations and maritime security driven by curiosity and the need for practical application in their work - the author advocates for older individuals to return to education believing that their experience can enrich discussions and challenge assumptions ultimately leading to better decision-making and governance i enrolled in three certificate courses at the development academy of the philippines they covered geopolitics international relations strategic futures oceans the law of the sea and maritime security attending these courses virtually became one of the most stimulating things i did this year i did not go back to school because i needed certificates missed homework or had suddenly developed a fondness for deadlines i was curious i wanted to understand what was happening in the world and why but there was a practical reason too i needed this knowledge for my work i wanted to ask better questions and give better advice about policies that matter people at work now come to me with questions about security not because i am an expert but because i am studying it curiosity is a wonderful thing but one has to be useful too abstract until in our maritime security course retired associate justice antonio carpio showed us historical maps they made me appreciate something deceptively simple geography is neither a blessing nor a curse we cannot push china farther north we cannot move taiwan farther south we cannot wish the south china sea away but geography should not determine a nation s fate a short basketball player cannot suddenly become six-foot-eight but he can learn to run faster pass better play stronger defense see the court differently and use what he has to his advantage countries have to do the same thing then came the law attorney fretti ganchoon senior state counsel at the department of justice gave us a terrific lecture on the oceans unclos united nations convention on the law of the sea and international law these can sound terribly abstract until a marine is struck in the head somebody loses a thumb or fishermen come home injured and their wives wonder whether on the next trip they might become widows attorney isabel cañaveral legal officer of the university of the philippines institute for maritime affairs and law of the sea took us through the maritime zones jurisdictions rights and obligations created by unclos after that an ocean no longer looked like empty blue space to me it had boundaries rights responsibilities and consequences simulating a crisis then florence principe gamboa managing editor of facts made us confront what happens when geography law and politics collide with an actual emergency she put us through a simulation involving the evacuation of filipinos from taiwan suddenly geopolitics became very real who is in charge do we know where our people are how do we move some filipinos out of taiwan if commercial flights stop which taiwanese agencies do we coordinate with how do we communicate with our people and our counterparts on the ground and perhaps the most important question has the evacuation plan actually been tested these are not minor operational details in a crisis they may determine whether a plan works at all a plan on paper is not enough discovering its weak points after the crisis begins is already too late that raised another question what if we could think about crises before they happened that was what the strategic futures and national security course taught by dr oliva domingo of the up national college of public administration and governance asked us to do choices that can change a future strategic foresight is not fortune-telling it is a disciplined way of looking at several plausible futures using what we know today while recognizing what we do not know i chose chronic kidney disease not because i wanted to turn kidneys into a security threat but because disease on a large enough scale affects a country s choices read opinion philippines peculiar health policy waiting until kidneys fail young people on dialysis will not be joining the armed forces or the coast guard and when government spends billions treating preventable disease those resources come from the same national budget that must also fund education infrastructure social protection and security my paper therefore was not really about kidneys it was about choices made early enough to change a future i developed several scenarios in the future i considered most desirable government acted much earlier preventing diabetes and hypertension regulating unhealthy food environments giving incentives to urban and town planners to create places where people could walk play and socialize and teaching children early about eating well and staying healthy by the time a problem becomes a crisis our choices have already narrowed and across all these subjects maps oceans evacuation plans chronic disease one issue kept returning governance security does not exist only at sea at a border or inside a military installation it depends on whether institutions work agencies speak to one another responsibilities are clear and whether somebody has thought about what happens on monday morning after the crisis erupts on sunday night i came away with a conviction that sounds almost embarrassingly ordinary grand strategies do not work unless somebody makes sure the operational details work too what older people bring to the classroom which brings me to the dap learning team led by dean alyn joy baltazar they worked quietly in the background making sure lecturers and students remained connected despite weak and unreliable internet schedules ran on time lectures were recorded transcribed and uploaded promptly submissions met deadlines and spotify somehow managed to play the coolest music during our breaks in class we talked about governance coordination and institutional capacity the dap learning team demonstrated all three without announcing that they were doing so these courses made me question assumptions test the logic of my own arguments discard ideas i had become too comfortable with and look at familiar problems differently i brought experience into the classroom not necessarily wisdom i have worked in policymaking and implementation nationally and internationally i have seen policies succeed and fail i have watched institutions evolve more importantly i have known people whose lives were affected by all of them experience changes the questions one asks i can still be impressed by an idea but i am much more interested now in whether it works who will implement it what happens when it reaches the bureaucracy what happens when conditions change and ultimately how will it make people s lives better that is why i hope more older filipinos return to classrooms we need places where generations can meet where experience encounters new knowledge where assumptions can be challenged and where people can disagree without pretending that anyone already has all the answers i went back to school because i was curious i also wanted to be useful i came away understanding something i had not expected education does not change the map it changes how we
